stimulus.text: Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil; in its worst state an intolerable one; for when we suffer, or are exposed to the same miseries by a government, which we might expect in a country without government, our calamity is heightened by reflecting that we furnish the means by which we suffer. Wherefore, security being the true design and end of government, it unanswerably follows that whatever form thereof appears most likely to ensure it to us, with the least expense and greatest benefit, is preferable to all others.
stimulus.source_note: Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776), abridged. Public domain.

books.section: B. Common Sense, the Declaration of Independence, and Republican Self-Government

stem: Common Sense sold more than 100,000 copies in its first three months. What best explains why Paine's pamphlet persuaded colonists whom Enlightenment treatises had not reached?

options.text: Paine wrote in plainspoken language ordinary colonists could follow
Paine was the first writer to argue that the colonies should separate from Britain
options.misconception: Paine was not the first to argue for separation — his gift was saying it plainly, not saying it first.

options.text: Paine's pamphlet was distributed free by the Continental Congress
options.misconception: Background: Congress did not distribute Common Sense free — it sold because readers wanted it, at a low price.

options.text: Paine wrote only for the wealthy merchants who led the colonial assemblies
options.misconception: Paine wrote for ordinary readers, not for an elite — his plain language is what carried the pamphlet so far.

rationales.A: Paine stated the argument for independence in plainspoken language — Background: the treatises spoke in lofty Enlightenment terms few colonists followed. Plain words reached readers the treatises never did.
rationales.B: Separation had been argued before Paine. His success was the plain language, not the first claim.
rationales.C: Congress did not hand the pamphlet out free. It sold more than 100,000 copies because ordinary readers bought it.
rationales.D: Paine's audience was the opposite of an elite. His pamphlet reached ordinary colonists precisely because it spoke plainly.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the sales. Background: more than 100,000 copies in three months means ordinary readers were buying it.
2. Ask what ordinary readers could follow. Background: the treatises spoke in lofty language; Paine's argument is plainspoken.
3. Name the difference. Paine translated the case for independence into words anyone could use.
Remember: an idea persuades a people when it is said in their language — plain words travel farther than learned ones.
